[01:25] Priya: (typing) Here is a sample prompt, we set temperature 0.2 for deterministic suggestions, max_tokens 64, and top_p 0.95. Watch the streaming chunks — you'll see partial tokens, then finalization at end.
[01:40] Rosa: So with streaming do we incur costs per chunk or per final token?
[01:45] Priya: Good question. Billing is per token consumed; streaming doesn't change billing. But because you can render partial results you can reduce perceived latency on the UI.
[01:57] Evelyn: Any rate limiting concerns if we do 50 rps from multiple regions?
[02:02] Jordan: Hosts have quotas and rate limits per API key and per account. For mid-market we recommend dedicated or higher quota packs. But for initial pilot hosted can easily handle 50rps — we can open limits as needed.
[02:15] Priya: I'm going to intentionally cause a simulated network drop mid-stream so you can see retry behavior. (typing) Ok here i issue a request with an idempotency-key header.
[02:30] Priya: When the client reconnects it will retry using the same idempotency-key. The server will either continue from last committed token or return the cached completion depending on timing.
[02:42] Marcus: Wait, so if we retry with same key do we ever double-charge?
[02:46] Priya: We protect against duplicate generation; we won't charge twice for the same logical completion if it was already persisted. There are edge cases — e.g., if the generate didn't commit results, then a retry may re-run inference and that counts. The safe pattern is: include idempotency-key plus a short TTL and monitor in console for dedup events.
[03:07] Rosa: How does the KV cache fit into this? Our prompts reuse a lot of system messages.
[03:12] Priya: We have automatic prefix/KV caching for sessions; that reduces per-token cost because the model doesn't have to re-encode repeated context. In logs you'll see cache hits. (note: auto-transcriber sometimes writes KV cash)
[03:25] Jordan: Quick note on parameters: lower temp + lower top_p increases determinism but may make replies more brittle. For triage we usually recommend temp 0.0-0.3 and top_p 0.8-0.95, and max_tokens tuned to expected reply length.
[03:40] Evelyn: Latency question again — our probe is P95 350ms. Do you have published numbers for the hosted stack at that size?
[03:48] Jordan: We publish performance profiles per model in the model catalog. For short sequences and small models p95 can be under 200ms in many regions, but ymmv — prompt prep, network, client rendering count. We'll run a 48-hour benchmark on your sample traffic to get real numbers.

[04:09] Priya: Sure. Here on the console trace you can see: request received, kernel selection, KV cache hit, token generation timeline, and token cost breakdown. We also surface per-token latency and the batching decisions.
[04:24] Priya: (click) I can also toggle to simulated heavy-load to show how the system batches requests — you'll see the batch size and how it affects per-token latency vs throughput.
[04:36] Rosa: Does batching increase tail latency?
[04:38] Priya: It can. Smart batching balances latency SLOs and throughput — you can pin per-route latency objectives and reduce batching for routes that need tight p95.
[04:49] Evelyn: Security — we need SSO and audit logs and customer-managed keys if possible. Are those available in hosted?
[04:56] Jordan: Hosted supports SAML SSO for the console and API tokens tied to teams. For cryptographic controls we integrate with KMS providers for key wrapping in Private deployments; hosted has managed keys but we provide envelope encryption and audit logs. For stricter controls we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) where customer-managed HSM/KMS is available.
[05:17] Marcus: What's the data retention for request/response logs? We need to ensure PHI is not retained beyond 30 days for the pilot.
[05:24] Jordan: Hosted has configurable retention; default is 90 days but we can set shorter retention windows for enterprise agreements and we can redact logs at ingest. We'll include that in the security pack.
[05:34] Priya: Back to retries, here's an example code snippet. (reads) Use idempotency-key: uuid.v4(), send request stream, if you lose the SSE connection, reconnect and pass same key. On the client we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and a max retry cap.
[05:50] Marcus: Any built-in server-side backpressure signals we can use?
[05:54] Priya: Yes we return 429s when the route is backpressured; the console also surfaces throttling per-route with suggested backoff. Also you can watch the route-level token and qps metrics.
[06:06] Rosa: Is there a way to do partial responses where we stop mid-generation because UI wants to present interim answer?
[06:11] Priya: Streaming supports chunked partial tokens. You can set stop tokens or stop conditions in the request to force generation end. Also you can set a max_time_ms to cap generation duration.
[06:22] Evelyn: For our audit and compliance team, we need proof that hosted meets SOC2 requirements.
[06:27] Jordan: We'll share our SOC2 report and summary of controls. Also include details on access logs, role-based access control, and encryption at rest/in transit.
[06:37] Marcus: Architecture question: if we need regional isolation for EU data, can hosted route only to eu-west?
[06:43] Jordan: Yes, you can pin requests by region using routing policies; the control plane supports region-specific endpoints and also fallback policies. For strict residency we'd recommend Private, but hosted supports region routing for EU, NA, APAC clusters.
[06:57] Priya: I want to show an intentional retry scenario now: issue request, drop connection, reissue with same idempotency-key. You can see in the trace the server returning a cached completion and the request labeled as deduped.
[07:12] Marcus: That dedupe label - ok. What about cost visibility per token at route level?
[07:18] Priya: The console has token-level cost breakdown and per-route cost rollups. You can also export CSV for chargeback.
[07:26] Rosa: For the product UX we might want to warm cache for common system prompts. Can we pre-seed the session?
[07:33] Priya: Yes, you can pre-warm the KV cache by sending a priming request or using the session warm API. That reduces first-call latency for common prompts.
[07:43] Evelyn: How do you recommend we handle hallucinations in the triage flow?
[07:48] Jordan: Multiple strategies: low temperature, system message instruction tuning, post-filter/reranking. Redwood supports reranking and a rerank endpoint; you can also send multiple short generations and pick the best via a scoring function.
[08:01] Marcus: Is reranking a dedicated call that increases cost?
[08:04] Priya: Yes it adds compute, so it's a tradeoff. We often recommend a lightweight heuristic first and serving rerank only for high-stakes replies.
[08:14] Rosa: Back to reliability — do you have graceful fallback patterns if model variant is unavailable?
[08:19] Priya: Yes our smart routing supports fallback to cheaper model variants or to a cached response tier. You can define fallback policies per route: for example, price-tier -> latency-tier -> cached-reply.
[08:32] Marcus: We're also concerned with idempotency across multi-turn sessions. If the user sends a confirm and we re-run a prompt, how do we ensure side-effects are exactly-once?
[08:41] Jordan: For side effects you should use a transaction layer in your app; keep model responses as advisory. For critical writes, double-check with a server-side idempotency guard keyed by business identifiers. Redwood's idempotency protects model generation but not downstream DB writes.
[09:00] Priya: Ok i want to show one more feature: streaming interim tokens with deterministic stop. (typing) Here we set max_tokens low and stop sequence to a newline. See how the stream closes early.
[09:18] Evelyn: Any gotchas with streaming and mobile clients with flaky networks?
[09:23] Priya: Mobile clients should implement incremental rendering and a reconnect strategy with same idempotency-key. We also recommend an offline fallback UI that explains partial completion might have happened.
